The structure is CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂Br: a four-carbon chain with a double bond and a bromine on
the end carbon.
Parent chain: 4 carbons containing the C=C ⇒ butene.
Now number the chain. IUPAC gives the lowest locant to the principal characteristic group or,
where the halogen is only a substituent, the lowest locants to the set as a whole.
Numbering from the CH₂Br end: Br on C1, double bond starting at C2 ⇒ locants {1, 2}.
Numbering from the CH₃ end: double bond starting at C2, Br on C4 ⇒ locants {2, 4}.
The first set is lower, so number from the bromine end.
That gives bromo at 1 and the ene at 2.
∴ 1-bromobut-2-ene.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|17||0|0:
Replacing Cl on a benzene ring is nucleophilic aromatic substitution, and it is hard because
the C–Cl bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring, and because the
ring is already electron rich and repels an incoming nucleophile.
Adding –NO₂ groups changes both things. The nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing by
−I and −R, so it pulls electron density *out* of the ring.
Crucially, it withdraws from the ortho and para positions specifically — those are the positions
whose resonance structures place the positive charge where the nitro group can stabilise it.
In 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene the chlorine is at C1, with nitro groups ortho (C2) and para (C4):
exactly the right places.
The intermediate Meisenheimer complex, carrying a negative charge, is therefore stabilised by
delocalisation onto the nitro oxygens, and the substitution proceeds easily.
∴ because –NO₂ withdraws electrons from the ortho and para positions.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|18||0|0:
Work through the sequence.
Ethanol + PCl₅ — the hydroxyl is replaced by chlorine:
X = CH₃CH₂Cl, chloroethane.
X + alcoholic KOH — alcoholic KOH favours elimination over substitution, so HCl is removed:
Y = CH₂=CH₂, ethene.
(Had it been aqueous KOH the product would have been ethanol again, which is the point of
specifying 'alc'.)
Y + conc. H₂SO₄ at room temperature — the acid adds across the double bond:
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ ⇒ CH₃CH₂OSO₃H, ethyl hydrogen sulphate.
Then H₂O with heat hydrolyses that ester back off:
CH₃CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O ⇒ CH₃CH₂OH + H₂SO₄
∴ Z is ethanol.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|19||0|0.s:
Compare how well each anion is stabilised once the proton is lost.
(1) Cl–CH₂CH₂–OH is an alcohol. Its alkoxide has the negative charge stuck on one oxygen with
no delocalisation; the chlorine's −I effect helps slightly, but alcohols remain far weaker acids
than phenols.
(2) Phenol gives phenoxide, where the charge is delocalised into the ring — already much better.
(4) The cresol has an electron-releasing –CH₃, which pushes charge back onto the oxygen and
destabilises the anion, so it is *less* acidic than phenol.
(3) The nitrophenol has –NO₂, strongly electron withdrawing by −I and −R. It accepts the
negative charge onto its own oxygens, giving by far the most stable anion.
So the order is alcohol < cresol < phenol < nitrophenol.
∴ the nitrophenol is most acidic.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|20||0|0.s:
Benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, has no α-hydrogen, so with concentrated alkali it cannot undergo an
aldol — instead it disproportionates. This is the Cannizzaro reaction.
One molecule is oxidised and another reduced:
2C₆H₅CHO + NaOH ⇒ C₆H₅COONa + C₆H₅CH₂OH
Now match the clues.
Product A is used as a food preservative ⇒ sodium benzoate, C₆H₅COONa ✓
Product B is described as aromatic, with OH on an sp³ carbon next to the ring. In benzyl alcohol,
C₆H₅CH₂OH, the OH sits on the CH₂ — an sp³ carbon — adjacent to the ring ✓
That description deliberately rules out phenol, where the OH is attached to an sp² ring carbon.
Phenyl methanol is simply the other name for benzyl alcohol.
∴ sodium benzoate and phenyl methanol.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|21||0|0.s:
In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction phenol is treated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH.
The alkali first removes a proton from CHCl₃ to give the CCl₃⁻ anion, which then loses Cl⁻:
CHCl₃ + OH⁻ ⇒ CCl₃⁻ + H₂O
CCl₃⁻ ⇒ :CCl₂ + Cl⁻
That :CCl₂ is dichlorocarbene — a neutral carbon with only six valence electrons, so it is
electron deficient and acts as the electrophile.
The phenoxide ion, which is electron rich, attacks it at the ortho position. Hydrolysis of the
resulting benzal chloride gives the aldehyde, so the product is salicylaldehyde.
(2) Kolbe's reaction uses CO₂ as the electrophile, (3) Friedel–Crafts acylation uses an acylium
ion, and (4) Fittig's reaction is a coupling with sodium, not an electrophilic attack.
∴ the Reimer–Tiemann reaction.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|22||0|0:
Ethanol with concentrated H₂SO₄ gives different products at different temperatures, and that
is exactly what the question is testing.
At about 140 °C with *excess ethanol*, two molecules condense and lose one water:
2C₂H₅OH ⇒ C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ + H₂O
This is intermolecular dehydration, and the product is ethoxyethane (diethyl ether).
At about 170 °C (443 K) with excess acid, a single molecule loses water internally:
C₂H₅OH ⇒ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
That is intramolecular dehydration, giving ethene — which is option (2), and the wrong product here.
So both the temperature and which reagent is in excess matter.
∴ by heating excess ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 140 °C.
